excerpt: Rapid Robotics rented pre-trained factory robot arms to manufacturers for about $25,000 a year. Funding history, how it worked, its current status and alternatives.
content:
Rapid Robotics was a Bay Area startup that tried to make factory automation as easy as hiring a temporary worker. Its product, the Rapid Machine Operator, was a six-joint robotic arm inside a safety work cell, with computer vision and an iPad for manual control. TechCrunch reported in 2020 that it handled tasks such as part inspection, injection-moulding machine tending, pick-and-place and welding, and that factories could rent it for around $25,000 a year. The company said the robot could be deployed in hours, without programming or robotics expertise, which is the robotics-as-a-service model.

Early customers named in TechCrunch's coverage included Westec Plastics, a Bay Area plastics moulder, and TruePill, a pharmacy company that used the robots to fill and label prescription bottles. The company also targeted the automotive sector.

Rapid Robotics raised money quickly. TechCrunch reported a $5.5 million seed round in November 2020, led by Greycroft and Bee Partners, and a $12 million Series A in April 2021 led by New Enterprise Associates. In August 2021 it raised a $36.7 million Series B co-led by Kleiner Perkins and Tiger Global, at a $192.5 million valuation, bringing total funding to $54.2 million. Jordan Kretchmer was CEO.

Current status: when we checked in October 2026, rapidrobotics.com redirected to a page offering the domain name for sale. We found no official announcement of a shutdown or acquisition, so treat the service as unavailable unless the company says otherwise. Manufacturers looking for similar rented or easy-to-deploy robots should consider the alternatives below.

This page is research, not a review. We have not used Rapid Robotics; facts come from the reporting under Sources and the company's archived website.
